title: Brass
objective: After this level you can explain how brass players change notes with their lips and valves.
summary: Brass players buzz their lips into a cup mouthpiece; lip tension picks notes of the harmonic series. Valves (about 1815) add tubing to fill the gaps; the trombone slides.

cards.headline: A bugle has no valves and no holes, yet it plays a tune.
cards.body: Nothing on it moves: it's a bent metal tube with a mouthpiece at one end. Every note it plays comes from the player's lips and a hidden ladder of notes built into the tube itself.

cards.headline: It starts with a buzz
cards.body: Press your lips together and blow until they buzz. That's a brass player's reed. The lips vibrate against a cup-shaped mouthpiece and set the air column in the tube vibrating. Tighten them and they spring back faster, so they buzz at a higher frequency and the note goes up.

cards.headline: The tube's hidden ladder
cards.body: A tube doesn't accept just any note. It favors a set called the harmonic series: frequencies at whole-number multiples of its lowest note, the fundamental. Two times is Level 8's octave; three and four times climb higher still. Without valves, those are the only notes a brass tube can play, and the player picks among them with lips and breath. That's the bugle's whole trick.

mascot.line: Hold on to this ladder. Level 20 uses it to explain why instruments sound different.

cards.headline: Valves: extra plumbing
cards.body: The ladder has gaps. Valves, invented about 1815, fill them: press one and the air takes a detour through extra tubing, so the tube gets longer and a lower ladder takes over. On a trumpet, the first valve lowers the note by a tone, the second by a semitone and the third by three semitones. The trombone skips valves and uses a slide, changing its length smoothly.

cards.headline: Brass: buzzed
learned: Lips buzz against a cup mouthpiece
Harmonic series: whole-number multiples of the fundamental
Valves (about 1815) add tubing; the trombone slides

questions.prompt: In a brass instrument, what makes the first vibration?

options.label: The player's lips buzzing against the mouthpiece
A cane reed clamped to the mouthpiece
options.rationale: Reeds belong to woodwinds like the clarinet.

options.label: Air blown against a sharp edge
A string stretched inside the bell

questions.explanation: Brass players buzz their lips against a cup-shaped mouthpiece, which sets the air column vibrating.

questions.prompt: A bugle has no valves or slide. How does a bugler play different notes?

options.label: By covering holes along the tube
By pulling out a hidden slide
By using lips and breath to pick notes of the harmonic series
By blowing harder on one single note
options.rationale: Blowing harder alone doesn't explain the different notes.

questions.explanation: Without valves, a brass tube plays only its harmonic series, and the player chooses among those notes with lips and breath.

questions.prompt: Level 13 said a woodwind's air column length sets its note. What does pressing a trumpet valve do?

options.label: Shortens the tube, so the notes rise
options.rationale: A valve adds tubing; it doesn't cut it.

options.label: Adds extra tubing, so the notes drop
Opens a hole, like a tone hole
options.rationale: Valves reroute the air through more tube.

options.label: Tightens the lips automatically
options.rationale: Valves change the tube, not the lips.

questions.explanation: A valve sends the air through extra tubing; the longer air column gives a lower set of notes.
